16.7.3 Physical Properties

With the exception of acetylene which has garlic like odour, all other alkynes are odourless and colourless.

The first three members (ethyne, propyne and butynes) are gases, next eight straight chain alkynes (C₅–C₁₂) are liquids and higher alkynes are solids at room temperature and pressure.

The boiling points of alkynes are slightly higher than the corresponding alkanes and alkenes and increase regularly with increase in the number of carbon atoms in the alkynes. However, their melting points do not follow a regular sequence. Instead, they change irregularly with increase in the number of carbon atoms (Table 16.4). Boiling points of terminal alkynes are lower than isomeric non-terminal alkynes.

Alkynes like alkanes and alkenes are non-polar; therefore, they are insoluble in water but readily dissolve in organic solvents such as ether, ethanol, acetone, carbon tetrachloride, benzene etc.

The density of alkynes increases with molecular mass. They are slightly denser than the corresponding alkanes and alkenes. All alkynes are lighter than water.

Table 16.4 Boiling and Melting Points of Some Alkynes

16.7.4 Relative Stabilities of alkynes

Like alkenes, the alkynes also exhibit stability to varying degree. The stability of alkynes, also depends on factors like position of the triple bond in the molecule and number and nature of the substituents attached to triple bonded carbon atoms. Generally non-terminal alkynes are relatively more stable than terminal alkynes.

The stabilities of various isomeric alkynes can be compared, by measuring their heats of hydrogenation or heats of combustion. Stable alkynes evolve small amount of heat upon combustion and hydrogenation and vice versa.

For example butyne has two isomers i.e. but-1-yne and but-2-yne. Upon hydrogenation but-1-yne releases large amount of heat than but-2-yne, therefore but-1-yne is less stable than but-2-yne.

16.7.5 Preparation of Alkynes by Elimination Reactions

Elimination reactions involve the removal of atoms or groups from two adjacent carbon atoms to form pi bond. This is also called 1,2-elimination or β-elimination (Section 17.1.7). These reactions result in the formation of unsaturated compounds. Alkyne can be prepared by the following elimination reactions.

16.7.5.1 Dehydrohalogenation of Vicinal Dihalides

Vicinal and geminal dihalides, when treated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide or sodium amide in liquid ammonia, form alkynes. It is a two step reaction. The elimination product of the first step (vinyl halide), is treated with stronger base such as sodium amide to remove another molecule of HX.

Figure 16.9 Orbital hybridization model of acetylene.

Thus, the carbon –carbon triple bond is made up of one sigma and two pi bonds. The acetylene molecule has linear geometry with H–C–C bond angle of 180°. The carbon–carbon triple bond length is 119 pm and that of C–H bond is 106 pm.

16.7.3 Physical Properties

With the exception of acetylene which has garlic like odour, all other alkynes are odourless and colourless.

The first three members (ethyne, propyne and butynes) are gases, next eight straight chain alkynes (C₅–C₁₂) are liquids and higher alkynes are solids at room temperature and pressure.

The boiling points of alkynes are slightly higher than the corresponding alkanes and alkenes and increase regularly with increase in the number of carbon atoms in the alkynes. However, their melting points do not follow a regular sequence. Instead, they change irregularly with increase in the number of carbon atoms (Table 16.4). Boiling points of terminal alkynes are lower than isomeric non-terminal alkynes.

Alkynes like alkanes and alkenes are non-polar; therefore, they are insoluble in water but readily dissolve in organic solvents such as ether, ethanol, acetone, carbon tetrachloride, benzene etc.

The density of alkynes increases with molecular mass. They are slightly denser than the corresponding alkanes and alkenes. All alkynes are lighter than water.

Table 16.4 Boiling and Melting Points of Some Alkynes

16.7.4 Relative Stabilities of alkynes

Like alkenes, the alkynes also exhibit stability to varying degree. The stability of alkynes, also depends on factors like position of the triple bond in the molecule and number and nature of the substituents attached to triple bonded carbon atoms. Generally non-terminal alkynes are relatively more stable than terminal alkynes.

The stabilities of various isomeric alkynes can be compared, by measuring their heats of hydrogenation or heats of combustion. Stable alkynes evolve small amount of heat upon combustion and hydrogenation and vice versa.

For example butyne has two isomers i.e. but-1-yne and but-2-yne. Upon hydrogenation but-1-yne releases large amount of heat than but-2-yne, therefore but-1-yne is less stable than but-2-yne.

16.7.5 Preparation of Alkynes by Elimination Reactions

Elimination reactions involve the removal of atoms or groups from two adjacent carbon atoms to form pi bond. This is also called 1,2-elimination or β-elimination (Section 17.1.7). These reactions result in the formation of unsaturated compounds. Alkyne can be prepared by the following elimination reactions.

16.7.5.1 Dehydrohalogenation of Vicinal Dihalides

Vicinal and geminal dihalides, when treated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide or sodium amide in liquid ammonia, form alkynes. It is a two step reaction. The elimination product of the first step (vinyl halide), is treated with stronger base such as sodium amide to remove another molecule of HX.
